il-17031-bos-matter-81238.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

COOK COUNTY PILOT PROGRAM FOR ACQUISITION OF TAX CERTIFICATES

WHEREAS, the Illinois General Assembly enacted Public Act 104-0553, establishing a pilot program that authorizes Cook County to directly acquire tax certificates for tax-delinquent properties; and

WHEREAS, the implementation of this pilot program will promote government transparency, protect vulnerable homeowners and help stabilize the property tax system within Cook County; and

WHEREAS, the pilot program allows Cook County, as Trustee under 35 ILCS 200/21-90, to acquire up to 100 tax certificates for properties offered at each of the first six annual tax sales to occur after the effective date of Public Act 104-0553 so long as, during the tax year for which judgment and order of sale was rendered, the properties received a general homestead exemption and were among the 100 lowest total tax amounts billed prior to adjustment by homestead exemptions; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to 35 ILCS 200/21-385(d), the Cook County Clerk is authorized to administer payment plans and waive interest for owners of tax delinquent properties in their respective redemption periods; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to 35 ILCS 200/21-191, Cook County must transmit to the Cook County Clerk and Cook County Treasurer a list of properties proposed for acquisition under the pilot program; and

WHEREAS, counties participating in the pilot program must submit an annual report to the Illinois General Assembly and the Illinois Department of Revenue no later than the third Wednesday of February of each year.

NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County President and the Cook County Board of Commissioners hereby formally adopts and authorizes the implementation of the Tax-Delinquent Property Pilot Program as established and authorized by Illinois Public Act 104-0553; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Bureau of Economic Development shall be the primary entity responsible for developing the necessary procedures and overseeing the implementation of the pilot program, with the County Clerk and Cook County Land Bank Authority performing their respective statutory roles in the tax redemption process; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Cook County, through its Bureau of Economic Development, shall acquire 100 tax certificates offered at each of the next 6 tax sales for properties which received a general homestead exemption and were among the 100 lowest total tax amounts billed prior to adjustment by homestead exemptions; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Clerk shall ensure that each tax certificate on a property participating in the pilot program is provided the opportunity to participate in a payment plan under 35 ILCS 200/21-385(d); and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Bureau of Economic Development, pursuant to 35 ILCS 200/21-192, shall submit the required annual report to the Illinois General Assembly and the Illinois Department of Revenue no later than the third Wednesday of February for each calendar year following the acquisition of tax certificates through the pilot program; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a copy of the report shall also be provided to the Cook County Board of Commissioners to receive and file.

il-17031-bos-matter-81239.title:
PROPOSED ORDINANCE AMENDMENT

PROHIBITING DISCLOSURE OF PERSONAL OR PRIVATE INFORMATION 

BE IT ORDAINED, by the Cook County Board of Commissioners, that Chapter 34 Finance, Article IV Procurement Code, Division 9 Contract Management, Section 34-303 of the Cook County Code is hereby amended as Follows:

Sec. 34-303.  Prohibiting disclosure of personal information.

The purpose of this section is to prohibit the disclosure of personal information or private information by County contractors or persons with access to said personal information and/or private information via County contracts. 

(a) 	The following words, terms, and phrases, when used in this Section shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section:

The term “personal information” has the meaning ascribed to that term in the Illinois Personal Information Protection Act, 815 ILCS 530/5.

The term “private information" has the meaning ascribed to that term in the Illinois Freedom of Information Act, 5 ILCS 140/2. 

The term “immigration agent” means an agent of federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement, federal Customs and Border Protection, or any similar or successor agency, or any other individual with the power to investigate, arrest, or detain individuals or manage custody of detained individuals for purposes of civil immigration enforcement while acting in that capacity or conducting investigations or enforcement pursuant to that power. 

The term “data broker” means a person that collects personal information or private information and resells or discloses that information to others for profit.

(b) 	County employees shall not disclose personal information or private information accessed through County responsibilities for immigration enforcement purposes absent a criminal warrant, or judicial court order, or as required by 8 U.S.C. § 1373.

(c) 	No County contractor or person shall disclose personal information or private information acquired from the County pursuant to a contract whether during the term of the contract or at any time thereafter, in the following manner:

(1)	 to immigration agents unless required pursuant to a criminal warrant, or judicial court order;

(2) 	to a data broker or for a commercial purpose unless authorized under County ordinance. 

(d) 	Any contractor or person which discloses or uses personal information and/or private information acquired from the County through a contract in violation of the requirements of Section (c) shall notify the relevant County using agency within five business days regarding the violation and the type of personal information and/or private information impacted. The contractor or person shall be required to: cease any further disclosures of the personal information and/or private information; comply with relevant legal requirements for unlawful disclosures of personal information and/or private information under State and federal law; and make best efforts to obligate any and all third parties to which the contractor or person disclosed data in violation of this section to permanently delete all such data.

(e) 	The Cook County Office of the Independent Inspector General (OIIG) may conduct periodic reviews to ensure compliance under this section including but not limited to whether personal information or private information has been disclosed in violation of section (c). The results of such review will be issued as an OIIG Public Statement so long as they meet the requirements for such; otherwise, the results will appear in the OIIG’s public Quarterly Report. The applicable using agency shall cooperate with the OIIG in conducting any such reviews to determine if a violation of this section has occurred.

(f) 	Any person whose personal information or private information has been used or disclosed by a contractor in violation of this Section shall have a private right of action against that contractor in a civil action for injunctive and declaratory relief together with costs and such reasonable attorney's fees as the court allows. 

Effective date:  This ordinance shall be in effect 60 days after adoption.

il-17031-bos-matter-81242.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RESOLUTION HONORING THE 80TH ANNIVERSARY OF SAINT SOPHIA BULGARIAN ORTHODOX CHURCH

WHEREAS, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church was established in 1946 and has served as one of the oldest and most enduring Bulgarian Orthodox institutions in the Chicago metropolitan area for the last eight decades, providing a spiritual home for generations of Bulgarian immigrants and their descendants; and 
 
WHEREAS, throughout its 80-year history, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church has played an important role not only as a place of worship, but also as a center for community life, preserving Bulgarian Orthodox faith, culture, traditions, and national heritage in Cook County and the greater Chicago area; and 
 
WHEREAS, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church maintains its spiritual connection with the Bulgarian Orthodox Church - Bulgarian Patriarchate and has contributed to preserving the religious traditions and identity of generations of Bulgarian Americans; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Church celebrates September 17, the Feast Day of the Holy Martyrs Sophia, Faith, Hope, and Love, as its patronal feast day, bringing together parishioners, families, and members of the wider Bulgarian American community; and 
 
WHEREAS, in 1975, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Sunday School was founded as part of the Church’s mission to educate younger generations, and for more than fifty years the school has provided instruction in the Bulgarian language, Bulgarian culture and traditions, and Orthodox Christian religious education, helping generations of Bulgarian American children maintain a meaningful connection with their ancestral heritage and faith; and 
 
WHEREAS, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church and its Sunday School have strengthened the cultural and social fabric of Cook County by fostering community, education, volunteerism, intergenerational ties, and the preservation of the Bulgarian American heritage that forms part of the rich diversity of Cook County; and 
 
WHEREAS, in 2026, parishioners, alumni, families, clergy, and friends of Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church gather to commemorate its 80th anniversary, honoring the generations who built and sustained the Church and reaffirming its continuing mission for future generations; 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby congratulates Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church on its 80th Anniversary and its outstanding spiritual, educational, cultural, and community contributions to Cook County, and extends its best wishes to the Church, Saint Sophia Bulgarian Sunday School, their clergy, teachers, parishioners, students, alumni, and supporters in the years ahead; and 
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a suitable copy of this Resolution be presented to Saint Sophia Bulgarian Orthodox Church in recognition of this historic milestone and its eight decades of service to the Bulgarian American community and to Cook County.

il-17031-bos-matter-81243.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RECOGNIZING GINA ROXAS, OAKTON COLLEGE'S DISTINGUISHED ALUMNI HONOREE 

WHEREAS, The Oakton Distinguished Alumni Award began in 1982 to provide examples of the college’s values “through professional excellence, community service, and overall achievement.”; and  
 
WHEREAS, this year’s Honorees are making an impact across a wide range of fields and communities and includes Executive Director of Trickster Cultural Center, Gina Roxas; and  
 
WHEREAS, Roxas, a citizen of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, has drawn on her background in environmental studies and her grandmother’s traditional teachings as she works to connect Indigenous knowledge and Western science to advance ecological stewardship and cultural resilience; and  
 
WHEREAS, under Roxas’ leadership, Trickster Cultural Center has amplified Native American voices through first-voice narratives, contemporary arts, and community education; and  
 
WHEREAS, Roxas has also guided land-based initiatives that revitalize traditional plant knowledge and connect healing, environmental justice, and self-determination across Native communities and collaborating institutions; and  

WHEREAS, Oakton celebrated its Honorees’ accomplished graduates at its 2026 Distinguished Alumni Awards Ceremony on September 10th; and  
 
WHEREAS, Cook County is home to the country’s third-largest urban Native American population as it stands on the lands of the Council of Three Fires-the Ojibwa, Ottawa and Potawatomi-as well as the Miami, Peoria, Ho-Chunk, Menominee, Sauk and Meskwaki peoples;  
 
WHEREAS, Roxas has also been a tireless supporter of the LGBTQ community by hosting the Northwest Pride Fest and has also continued Trickster’s tradition of being a key early voting location; and   
 
WHEREAS, Roxas has served as a dedicated community partner with the office and community of the 15th District of Cook County, and under her leadership, they have held town halls, veterans resource programs, and other programming for the residents of the 15th District and county-wide; and    
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby congratulate Gina Roxas on being named as an Honoree of Oakton College’s Distinguished Alumni Award and thank her for her wonderful work connecting Indigenous wisdom and Western science and her advancement of ecological stewardship and cultural resilience; and 
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that suitable copies of this resolution be tendered to Gina Roxas in recognition of all her amazing contributions to her community and across the County.

il-17031-bos-matter-81244.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

A RESOLUTION REMEMBERING GOLDEN “GULAB” SINGH 

WHEREAS, Golden “Gulab” Singh was a legendary Indian veteran track and field athlete who achieved extraordinary success in international masters athletics after the age of 75, representing India with distinction and earning 41 gold, 6 silver, and 3 bronze medals; and 
 
WHEREAS, born in 1905 in Sirsa, Haryana, India, Singh served in the military and retired as a Nayab Subedar from the Burma Army in 1946, later serving as a physical training instructor in Haryana schools from 1947 to 1960; and 
 
WHEREAS, Singh entered international masters competition in 1981 at approximately 76 years of age and went on to establish four world records, competing internationally in the triple jump, long jump, high jump, sprints, discus, and other events; and 
 
WHEREAS, at the 1987 World Masters Championships in Melbourne, Australia, Singh set an M80 triple jump world record of 8.29 meters, further establishing his remarkable place in masters athletics history; and 
 
WHEREAS, his extraordinary life remains an enduring example of perseverance, discipline, service, courage, and excellence, inspiring athletes, seniors, the Indian diaspora, and future generations around the world; and 
 
WHEREAS, Adbhhut Media - Newspaper & Channel and the Midwest Punjabi Association (MPA), founded by Gurmeet Singh Dhalwan, are committed to preserving meaningful legacies, promoting cultural heritage, recognizing extraordinary individuals, and strengthening communities; and 
 
WHEREAS, Gurmeet Singh Dhalwan, Founder President; Prachi Jaitly, General Secretary; and Jasbir Kaur Mann, Advisory Board Member of the Midwest Punjabi Association (MPA), proudly join in recognizing and honoring the extraordinary life and legacy of Golden “Gulab” Singh; 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the life, historic athletic achievements, and enduring legacy of Golden “Gulab” Singh be recognized and honored with admiration, respect, and pride, and that his example continue to inspire generations to pursue excellence regardless of age or circumstance; and 

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this recognition is respectfully presented to his daughter, Varinder Kaur, and his son, Manjeet Singh, in honor of their father’s extraordinary life and legacy, so that his memory and achievements may continue to be celebrated for generations to come.

il-17031-bos-matter-81245.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RECOGNIZING SEPTEMBER AS SUICIDE PREVENTION MONTH IN COOK COUNTY 

WHEREAS, Suicide Prevention Month is observed every September as an opportunity to raise awareness about suicide prevention, reduce stigma around mental health issues, and to encourage open conversations and support for those affected by suicide; and  
 
WHEREAS, though Suicide Prevention Month began in 2008, the observance evolved over time through the efforts of mental health advocates, nonprofit organizations, and government agencies; and  
 
WHEREAS, this development began in 1975 thanks to activities sponsored by The American Association of Suicidology that culminated in the observance of National Suicide Prevention Week during the second full week of September, and was designed to inform and engage health professionals and the general public about suicide prevention and warning signs of suicide; and  
 
WHEREAS, later in 1999, U.S. Surgeon General Dr. David Satcher put out his Call to Action to Prevent Suicide, marking one of the earliest comprehensive efforts by the U.S. government to recognize suicide as a serious public health issue; and  
 
WHEREAS, then in 2001 the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration and the Office of the U.S. Surgeon General launched the National Strategy for Suicide Prevention, which became the blueprint for national suicide prevention efforts; and  
 
WHEREAS, the first Recognized Suicide Prevention Day was observed on September 10, 2003, as a result of the collaboration between The International Association for Suicide Prevention and the World Health Organization; and  
 
WHEREAS, on January 1, 2005, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline launched with a federal grant from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, and would go on to establish 109 call centers and become known as the country’s reliable resource for those in suicidal crisis - with 2.2 million calls being answered annually by 2018; and  
 
WHEREAS, on July 16, 2020, the FCC adopted rules to establish 988 as the nationwide, easy-to-remember 3-digit dialing code for people in crisis to connect with suicide prevention and mental health crisis counselors, and later that October the National Suicide Hotline Designation Act of 2020 was signed into law, incorporating 988 into statute as the new 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and Veterans Crisis Line phone number; and  
 
WHEREAS, since its official launch in July 2022, the 988 Lifeline has answered over 13 million calls, texts, and chats from people in need of support across the US and its territories; and  

WHEREAS, despite these advancements in resources and awareness, suicide continues be a prevalent concern both in the United States and worldwide; and  
 
WHEREAS, suicide is the third leading cause of death among 15-29-year-olds worldwide; and  
 
WHEREAS, every year over 700,000 people take their own life, one every 40 seconds, with many more who make suicide attempts; and  
 
WHEREAS, 5.5 percent of U.S. adults have serious thoughts of suicide each year; and  
 
WHEREAS, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there were 1,426 deaths by suicide in Illinois in 2024, or about 10.8 deaths for every 100,000 people in Illinois; and  
 
WHEREAS, according to the Cook County Department of Public Health’s (CCDPH) 2025 Suburban Cook County Suicide Report, there were a total of 267 suicide deaths in 2023, with a notable increase in suicide rates among Black and Hispanic residents from 2018; and  
 
WHEREAS, Black residents rate of deaths by suicide more than doubled in 2023 with 41 deaths compared to 18 in 2018; and  
 
WHEREAS, Hispanic residents rate of deaths by suicide also nearly doubled with only 23 deaths in 2018 compared to 39 in 2023; and  
 
WHERRAS, CCDPH’s report also found that Black high school students in suburban Cook County attempted suicide at three times the rate of their peers, while female teens were nearly three times as likely to visit the emergency department for suicide compared to their male peers; and  
 
WHEREAS, according to the CDC, risk factors that increase the likelihood of suicide include financial problems or job loss, lack of access to health care, partner or family relationship problems, and bullying or social isolation; and  
 
WHEREAS, suicide is preventable and there are actions and conditions that we as individuals and as a community can make to help protect those in mental crisis; and  
 
WHEREAS, such actions include creating access to affordable and high-quality health care, promoting connection across our communities, reducing the stigma of discussing mental health concerns, and serving as a supportive friend, partner, or family member to those experiencing mental health concerns; and  
 
WHEREAS, in order to better serve the mental health needs across Cook County, The Cook County Office of Behavioral Health was established by Cook County Health in 2023, particularly those from historically marginalized and underserved populations; and 
 
WHEREAS, if you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide or experiencing a mental health or substance use crisis, please call 988 to get connected to free, confidential support;  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby recognize September as Suicide Prevention Month in Cook County and encourage all to engage in conversations and actions that help mitigate the stigma and rate of suicide across Cook County, Illinois, and worldwide.

il-17031-bos-matter-81246.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

 RECOGNIZING SEPTEMBER AS RECOVERY MONTH IN COOK COUNTY 

WHEREAS, according to the 2024 United States National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 48.4 million (16.8%) Americans aged 12 and older battled a substance use disorder in 2024; and  
 
WHEREAS, the Survey also found that, in 2024, 27.9 million Americans 12 and older had an alcohol use disorder while 28.2 million Americans 12 or older has reported battling a drug use disorder in the past year; and  
 
WHEREAS, 1 in 6 (7.7 million) of these people who suffered from Substance Abuse Disorders (SUD) in the past year struggled with both alcohol and drug use disorders simultaneously; and  
 
WHEREAS, in 2024, 21.2 million adults suffered from both a mental health disorder and a substance use disorder; and  
 
WHEREAS, though genetics - including the impact of one’s environment on gene expression - account for about 40% to 60% of a person’s risk of addiction, other environmental factors that may increase a person’s risk of addiction include a chaotic home environment and use, parental drug use and attitude towards drugs, peer influences, community attitudes toward drugs, and poor academic achievement; and  
 
WHEREAS, substance use disorder doesn’t discriminate, and people from all walks of life - regardless of age, gender, cultural background, or socioeconomic status - can experience addiction; and  
 
WHEREAS, since 1989, Recovery Month has been observed every September to celebrate the gains and achievements made by those in recovery from substance use disorder; and 
 
WHEREAS, each September, thousands of prevention, treatment, and recovery programs and facilities around the country celebrate Recovery Month and speak about strides made by those in recovery and share their success stories with their neighbors, friends, and colleagues; and  
 
WHEREAS, this year's theme, "Recovery is REAL (Restoring Every Aspect of Life)", emphasizes that with the right treatment, support, and resources, recovery is possible; and  
 
WHEREAS, recovery is characterized by continual growth and improvement in one’s health and wellness, managing setbacks, and developing resilience to those setbacks; and  
 
WHEREAS, the process of recovery is highly personal and can include clinical treatment, medications, faith-based approaches, peer support, family support, self-care, and other approaches; and  
 
WHEREAS, The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration identifies four major dimensions of recovery; and  
 
WHEREAS, the first of these dimensions is health, meaning making informed, healthy choices that support physical and emotional well-being and overcoming or managing one’s disease and/or symptoms such as abstaining from use of alcohol, illicit drugs, and non-prescribed medication if one has an addiction problem; and  
 
WHEREAS, the second of these dimensions is home, ensuring that those in recovery have a stable and safe place to live; and  
 
WHEREAS, the third of these dimensions is purpose, meaning conducting meaningful daily activities including a job, school volunteerism, family caretaking, or creative endeavors, and the independence, income, and resources to participate in society; and  
 
WHEREAS, the final dimension of recovery is community, meaning having relationships and social networks that provide support, friendship, love, and hope 
 
WHEREAS, throughout National Recovery Month, we celebrate the more than 23 million Americans who have found a pathway from addiction to recovery as well as the family, friends, medical professionals, and advocates who help those in recovery reclaim their lives; and  
 
WHEREAS, in 2024, an estimated 18.2% of people aged 12 and older (52.6 million people) needed treatment for a substance use disorder in the past year, yet only 23% of those received the treatment needed; and  
 
WHEREAS, it is vital for those in recovery that communities, advocates, organizations, and government agencies remain steadfast in their commitment to creating access to affordable recovery programs and treatments; and  
 
WHEREAS, Cook County’s dedication to ensuring its residents have such access can be found through its Cook County Health’s Bridge Clinic at Cook County Health at the Ruth M. Rothstein CORE Center (2020 W Harrison St. Chicago IL 60612) offers rapid evaluation and treatment for patients struggling with addiction with no appointment needed;  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby recognize September as National Recovery Month and celebrates all those who have worked or are currently working towards their recovery from addiction as well as the family, friends, and medical teams who make such recovery possible.

il-17031-bos-matter-81247.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

A RESOLUTION RECOGNIZING THE WEEK OF OCTOBER 11TH AS EMERGENCY NURSES WEEK 

WHEREAS, since 1989, the Emergency Nurses Association has recognized the second Wednesday in October as Emergency Nurses Day; and  
 
WHEREAS, in 2001, the Emergency Nurses Association expanded the celebration to a full week to highlight emergency nurses more; and 
 
WHEREAS, this year’s Emergency Nurse’s Week will be observed during the week of October 11th; and 
 
WHEREAS, tens of thousands of emergency nurses in the United States have expertise in caring for all emergency patients across the spectrum of the lifespan ushering life in at birth and allowing for a dignified death; and 
 
WHEREAS, emergency nurses are highly trained to recognize life-threatening problems and solve them on the spot, playing a vital role in treating patients in emergency situations, caring for those most in need, and saving lives on a daily basis; and 
 
WHEREAS, emergency nurses continue to stand strong no matter the challenges they face or the difficult situations that are brought to them; and 
 
WHEREAS, these characteristics provide a broad scope of practice for the delivery of critical and complex care within a limited timeframe to health care consumers of all ages and backgrounds; and  
 
WHEREAS, emergency nurses integrate critical thinking skills and knowledge of evidence-based practice into their delivery of care and decision-making; and 
 
WHEREAS, through research, education, and emergency nursing advocacy, the Emergency Nurses Association (ENA) supports and honors the advancement of professionalism of emergency nurses everywhere; and 
 
WHEREAS, ENA, the ENA Foundation, and other groups around our country have joined together to honor the extraordinary acts of service, compassion, and commitment that emergency nurses provide to patients every day; and  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby recognize the week of October 11th as Emergency Nurses Week in thanks to all the emergency nurses within the Cook County Health System and across the County for all their tireless dedication to ensuring emergency patients receive the treatment they need.

il-17031-bos-matter-81248.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

HONORING NATIONAL HISPANIC AND LATINX/E HERITAGE MONTH
 
WHEREAS, National Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage Month was founded to celebrate the diverse culture, extensive histories, and significant contributions of Hispanic and Latinx/e communities and takes place on a yearly basis from September 15th to October 15th; and
 
WHEREAS, Public Law 90-48 was passed in 1968 under President Lyndon Johnson, which celebrated one week of Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage; and
 
WHEREAS, with the passage of Public Law 100-402, it was extended to a month in 1988 by President Ronald Reagan and was enacted into law on August 17, 1988; and
 
WHEREAS, the independence of Guatemala, Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua, and El Salvador is celebrated on September 15th, followed by Mexico on September 16th, Chile on September 18th, and Belize on September 21st; and
 
WHEREAS, throughout the years, Hispanic and Latinx/e individuals have made notable cultural, economic, political and social contributions to the United States; and
 
WHEREAS, Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage Month is celebrated nationwide through community gatherings, cultural events, festivals, and educational programs; and
 
WHEREAS, Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage Month allows individuals to share their culture with one another and with the rest of the nation; and
 
WHEREAS, the population of Hispanic and Latinx/e people has increased over the years, with many arriving in large numbers to seek opportunities and work a variety of jobs, which have helped build and sustain this nation; and
 
WHEREAS, programs such as the Bracero Program in 1942 allowed Hispanics/Latinxs/es to migrate to the United States and work jobs that played an essential role in the economy; and
 
WHEREAS, according to the Pew Research Center, about 20% of the population in the United States is Hispanic, making it the second largest racial/ethnic group in the country; and

WHEREAS, Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage Month acknowledges Hispanic leaders who have organized and fought for equal justice to ensure that all have an opportunity to thrive and grow; and
 
WHEREAS, the Hispanic and Latinx/e community is rich with activists, leaders, and community members who have fought on issues ranging from labor to immigration to environmental justice and more; and
 
WHEREAS, since January 2025, the Hispanic and Latinx/e community has been especially vulnerable to increased attacks from the federal governments, sparked by increased patrolling of immigration federal agents and a recent Supreme Court case that allows agents to stop individuals based on race, language, and occupation; and
 
WHEREAS, the Hispanic and Latinx/e community in Cook County has organized themselves to defend against deportations and violations of due process and uplift their constitutional rights; and
 
WHEREAS, Cook County is home to about 1.38 million Hispanic/Latinx/e residents, many of which reside in and shape vibrant communities throughout the County, such as Little Village, Pilsen, Melrose Park, Berwyn, Southeast Chicago, Albany Park, Logan Square, and Humboldt Park; and

NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners recognizes September 15th to October 15th as National Hispanic and Latinx/e Heritage Month to celebrate the work and dedication to the United States.

il-17031-bos-matter-81251.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT COMMUNITY AND ETHNIC MEDIA ACROSS COOK COUNTY 

WHEREAS, Cook County recognizes that information is power, and that community and ethnic media play a vital role in ensuring equitable, local and culturally and linguistically relevant and trusted information to communities that are often not reached by mainstream media; and 

WHEREAS, Cook County is the second largest county in the country that is home to diverse racial, ethnic, religious and linguistic communities; and 

WHEREAS, community media refers to independent media organizations that are owned, controlled, and operated by and for a community, serving its specific interests. They serve as a third sector of the media apart from mainstream private and public media, fostering media pluralism and supporting democratic functions including voter education, civic engagement, participation and access; and 

WHEREAS, ethnic media refers to media that is developed by and for specific ethnic, religious or linguistic communities, that are often isolated from mainstream media. They provide culturally relevant news and information, often in their respective languages; and 

WHEREAS, Cook County is committed to ensuring all residents and communities have access to culturally relevant, and linguistically accessible information about our social support programs, small business grants, public health information, and other opportunities; and 

WHEREAS, Cook County recognizes that partnering with community and ethnic media can help ensure more residents, businesses and communities have access to Cook County resources and information; and

WHEREAS, Cook County recognizes that a healthy democracy depends on a diverse and independent media landscape in which communities have the opportunity to tell their own stories, elevate issues that matter to their residents, hold institutions accountable, and participate fully in civic life; and

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Cook County will launch a series of engagements with community and ethnic media starting with President Preckwinkle’s Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Address and over the next year and into the future.

il-17031-bos-matter-81253.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

CELEBRATING THE TENURE OF STATE SENATOR LAURA FINE 
 
WHEREAS, State Senator Laura Fine is a lifelong Glenview resident and dedicated public servant; and 
 
WHEREAS, Senator Fine’s story of civil service began when she obtained her B.A. in telecommunications from Indiana University, followed by an M.A. in political science from Northeastern Illinois University; and 

WHEREAS, Senator Fine’s dedication to public service was evident from the beginning of her career, including her first work as a journalist in radio and television news for media outlets throughout the Midwest, as well as her service as a professor at Northeastern University, where she taught courses in the study of the Constitution and other areas of political science; and 
 
WHEREAS, Senator Fine first held elected office in 2009 when she served as Northfield Township Clerk, a position she held through 2012; and 
 
WHEREAS, following her tenure as Northfield Township Clerk, Senator Fine represented the 17th District of the Illinois House of Representatives beginning in 2013 to 2019, the decision to run spurred on by a battle with a health insurance company following a car accident; and 
 
WHEREAS, Senator Fine has proudly served the 9th Senate District since January 6, 2019, where she is a member of several Illinois Senate committees including Chair of the Behavioral and Mental Health Committee, vice-Chair of the Insurance Committee, Environment and Conservation, Health and Human Services, Judiciary, Public Health, and Worker’s Compensation; and 

WHEREAS, Senator Fine is a known advocate for the environment and consumer safety, passing legislation reducing plastic pollution, reducing the use of “forever chemicals” and protecting children by ensuring baby food is free of toxic heavy metals; and 

WHEREAS, Senator Fine is an ally of the LGBTQIA+ community, passing legislation that made it easier for transgender individuals to change their gender designation on their birth certificates and expanded access to infertility treatments for LGBTQIA+ couples; and 

WHEREAS, Senator Fine has tirelessly championed efforts to make healthcare more affordable and accessible by advancing legislation to expand insurance coverage requirements, strengthen the Illinois Department of Insurance’s authority to reject unjustified rate increases, and increase transparency for consumers when selecting and purchasing health insurance plans; and 
 
WHEREAS, as Chair of the Behavioral and Mental Health Committee, she has made it her mission to reduce the stigma surrounding mental healthcare, expand access to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and ensure that mental healthcare is covered by insurance on equal terms with physical healthcare; and 
 
WHEREAS, Senator Fine is woven into the fabric of the community as an active member of Kiwanis Club of Glenview-Northbrook, the Rotary Club of Glenview Sunrise, and the Glenview/Glencoe League of Women Voters; and 
 
WHEREAS, most recently Senator Fine was elected chair of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Legislative Caucus a binational, nonpartisan organization of state and provincial legislators passionate about policies to protect and restore the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River basin; and 
 
WHEREAS, Senator Fine is lauded for her leadership and dedication to the betterment of the lives of Illinois residents; and 
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby honor and celebrate Senator Fine’s nearly two decades of tireless work on behalf of her constituency; and 
  
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a suitable copy of this Resolution be spread upon the official proceedings of this Honorable Body and that a suitable copy of this Resolution be tendered to Senator Fine as a means of conveying our gratitude and appreciation for her years of dedicated service.

il-17031-bos-matter-81254.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

CELEBRATING MICHAEL KRELOFF’S 80TH BIRTHDAY 

WHEREAS, lifelong Cook County resident, and 14th District denizen, Michael Kreloff is celebrating his 80th birthday; and
 
WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff was born on September 24, 1946, at Lincoln Park’s Grant Hospital, spending his formative years in Edgewater and Skokie; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff has long been involved in the betterment of society, becoming involved in the 1960s peace movement during his college years; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff obtained both his Bachelor of Science and Juris Doctor from the University of Illinois, specializing in the field of State and Local Government Election Law; and  

WHEREAS, during his college tenure Micheal Kreloff worked on campaigns for Eugene McCarthy, Harold Washington, Paul Simon, and Barack Obama to name a few; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff was admitted to the Illinois Bar in 1971; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff continued his adult years living across Cook County, including in Rogers Park, Northfield, and Northbrook; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff and his wife, Nancy, raised two wonderful daughters, Lori and Lynn; and  

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff’s service to Cook County has been vast and impactful; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff was an Assistant States Attorney under Bernard Carey and Richard M. Daley, primarily in the Election Law Division; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff served as the Chair of the Cook County Judicial Advisory Board from 1987 to 1991; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff was Secretary of the County Board under President Phelan, where he worked to reinstate abortions at Cook County Hospital; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff worked to pass the Motor Voter Act of Illinois in 2016 with then Cook County Clerk David Orr, helping to sign up more than 1 million eligible but unregistered Illinoisans; and
 
WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff is a fierce advocate for the right to vote with decades-long dedication to political activism; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff passionately served as Northfield Township Committeeperson beginning in 2002, until he retired in 2018; and 

WHEREAS, Michael Kreloff retired from the practice of law at the end of December 2024, but remains know to all for his warmth, kindness, intellect, and resolve; and 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby celebrate Michael Kreloff on the occasion of his 80th birthday and extends heartfelt gratitude for his lifetime of service and dedication to community; and 
  
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this text be spread upon the official proceedings of this Honorable Body, and a suitable copy be tendered to Michael Kreloff as a symbol of congratulations on this milestone.

il-17031-bos-matter-81256.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

HONORING REVEREND DR. TRUNELL D. FELDER ON HIS 25TH PASTORAL ANNIVERSARY AND NEW FAITH BAPTIST CHURCH INTERNATIONAL ON THEIR 50TH ANNIVERSARY

WHEREAS, on January 4, 1976, New Faith Baptist Church held its first worship service with 67 people at Blackhawk Elementary School in Park Forest. After studying the Park Forest area, the Reverend Junius Dudley found integrated churches, but he also recognized that they did not fully include the Black worship experience and lacked Black leadership. Concerned about the community, Reverend Dudley appealed to the Reverend Dale Cross of the Southern Baptist Convention for resources to establish a church. New Faith began as a Southern Baptist mission, with supplemental support for the pastor and access to the Convention's resources; and 
 
WHEREAS, New Faith grew rapidly and reached approximately 150 members, and although Reverend Dudley resigned in December 1978, his obedience and founding vision created a legacy that would continue for generations; and 
 
WHEREAS, on October 12, 1984, the church broke ground for a permanent facility, beginning a lasting ministry presence in Matteson, and on February 22, 1987, New Faith moved into its permanent home at 25 South Central Avenue in Matteson with 287 members; Reverend Frank A. Thomas, New Faith’s 3rd Pastor, affectionately known as Pastor Frank, emphasized prayer, biblical teaching, and passionate preaching; and 
 
WHEREAS, as membership grew, New Faith expanded its staff by adding a Minister of Pastoral Care and a Minister of Music, and by 1990, New Faith had added a Director of Administration and a Youth Director; and 
 
WHEREAS, in September 1990, the church purchased an additional 22 acres, bringing its total land ownership to 27 acres, and Ministry opportunities for women, children, and men expanded, and the all-male ensemble Barnabas debuted during the 1990 revival. By 1991, New Faith had added a second worship service; and 
 
WHEREAS, in March 1992, New Faith had added a Saturday evening service, bringing the church to three weekly worship services. Growth required creative partnerships: the nursery operated at a nearby KinderCare, while Children's Church and Sunday school classes met at Woodgate School. The church added leadership positions in Christian education, justice, youth and family ministry, youth programming, and youth spiritual life. Programs such as Victorious Christian Living Institute, Jesus and Me, and Helping Young People Excel strengthened biblical education and youth development; and 
 
WHEREAS, with more than 52 ministries, over 2,000 members, and approximately 40 employees, New Faith began planning a major expansion. In October 1992, members contributed $101,245 toward the final payment on the 22-acre land acquisition and completed a sanctuary renovation after temporarily worshiping at Rich Central High School, a period that helped draw more young people to the ministry. The renovated sanctuary seated 960 people, and the church also built the Keith Sallie Activity Center, including classrooms, gathering space, reception areas, and additional washrooms; and 
 
WHEREAS, the center honored Keith Sallie, a young music director who encouraged young people to use their gifts for God's glory and whose life ended tragically in an automobile accident and the Wall of Recognition was installed in the Keith Sallie Activity Center to honor those whose sacrificial giving supported the building program. Harvey Hall was named for Kenneth Harvey, an award-winning media professional and faithful New Faith member who died in 1998; and 
 
WHEREAS, after 17 years of pastoral leadership, the Reverend Frank A. Thomas resigned in 1999 to become pastor of Mississippi Boulevard Christian Church in Memphis, Tennessee. Following two years of prayer and fasting, New Faith called the Reverend Dr. Trunell D. Felder, then co-pastor of Ray of Hope Christian Church in Decatur, Georgia. His first sermon at New Faith, “Living for an Audience of One”, affirmed his call as a shepherd and lead servant. On July 28, 2001, the congregation assembled to vote, and in August 2001 the active membership confirmed Pastor Felder by a large majority; and 
 
WHEREAS, on January 13, 2002, Pastor Felder introduced a renewed vision and mission for New Faith Baptist Church. Membership grew from approximately 2,200 to more than 6,000, requiring four worship services each weekend. Evangelism and outreach became central priorities. In Ford Heights, one of Illinois' most economically distressed communities, New Faith provided health screenings, school and baby supplies, resident care packages, a job fair, a carnival, and a gospel concert; and 
 
WHEREAS, in 2005, New Faith Baptist Church became New Faith Baptist Church International. Its global ministry expanded to 15 locations in Ghana and six locations in Cape Town, with outreach that supported churches, clean-water wells, schools, medical clinics, farms, orphan feeding programs, and Bible distribution across Africa, India, and China. Following Hurricane Katrina, New Faith became a major collection and distribution center, operating with around-the-clock volunteers to receive donations, coordinate shelter, pack supplies, and deliver truckloads of assistance to survivors in Texas. This response prepared the church for later disaster-relief efforts in Haiti in 2010 and Alabama in 2011; and 
 
WHEREAS, on June 1, 2012, New Faith opened a new sanctuary after years of prayer, fasting, and sacrificial giving. The expanded campus increased the church's capacity to worship, serve, and care for the community. By this period, New Faith's ministry and outreach had reached approximately 375,000 people worldwide; and 
 
WHEREAS, New Faith continued to broaden the meaning of ministry and community service. Its Expungement Fair became the largest event of its kind in Cook County's south suburbs at that time, bringing together legal, political, and community leaders to help residents address criminal records and avoid significant private legal costs. The church also partnered with Habitat for Humanity through homeownership workshops, financial support, and volunteer assistance, including support for a home built for a family of 20. Through Pastor Felder's leadership, New Faith also launched evangelism training through Won by One; and 
 
WHEREAS, under the theme New Faith New You, the church celebrated Pastor Felder's 60th birthday and another year of his devoted leadership. New Faith expanded family-centered gatherings, including Steppers Night Under the Stars, weekend game nights, and basketball camps, creating accessible opportunities for neighbors and visitors to experience fellowship and the love of Christ; and 
 
WHEREAS, New Faith has experienced continued growth and connection and created 12 new Unity Groups so members could build relationships and fellowship beyond the Sunday worship experience. Participation remains strong across women's, men's, youth, and senior ministries. The church reported more than 18,325 professions of faith and increased participation in Sunday school, Vacation Bible School, and volunteer outreach; and 
 
WHEREAS, New Faith Baptist Church International celebrates 50 years of worship, witness, and wondrous works, while the Reverend Dr. Trunell D. Felder celebrates 25 years of pastoral leadership. The church recognizes this milestone as its Year of Jubilee and gives thanks for a legacy that has grown from 67 worshipers in an elementary school into a local, national, and international ministry committed to faith, service, justice, education, family, and community transformation;  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the President and Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby recognize and commemorate the 25th Pastoral Anniversary of Reverend Dr. Trunell D. Felder and the 50th Anniversary of New Faith Baptist Church International; and 
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this Honorable Body extends its sincere congratulations and gratitude to Reverend Dr. Trunell D. Felder for his many years of faithful service to his church and the broader community and New Faith Baptist Church International on the occasion of its 50th Anniversary; and 
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this resolution be entered into the official proceedings of this Honorable Body, and that a suitable copy be presented to Reverend Dr. Trunell D. Felder as a token of respect and esteem.

il-17031-bos-matter-81258.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RESOLUTION COMMEMORATING THE 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF UNITED NATIONS WORLD CONFERENCE AGAINST RACISM IN DURBAN, SOUTH AFRICA

WHEREAS, this year marks the 25th Anniversary of The United Nations held the World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance (WCAR) in Durban, South Africa, and 

WHEREAS, over 16,000 people from across the globe attended the WCAR including 2,500 delegates from 170 countries, 4,000 civil society and non-governmental organization members, and 1,300 journalists and media staff; and

WHEREAS, one of the outcomes of the WCAR was The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA) which established a landmark international consensus framework to combat racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance; and 

WHEREAS, the work from the WCAR continues to live in communities across Cook County including the first municipal reparations program in the country passed in Evanston, Illinois; and

WHEREAS, the 25th Anniversary of the WCAR serves as an international day of remembrance, reflection, and mobilization that has been celebrated in Cook County, and around the world; and

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Board of Commissioners of Cook County hereby commemorates the 25th Anniversary of the World Conference Against Racism; and
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a suitable copy of this Resolution be provided to Cook County leaders who attended the WCAR as an honorable expression of appreciation for their work.
